claim: By 2029, we will deliver IBM Quantum Starling — a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum gates on 200 logical qubits
source_title: How IBM will build the world's first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer
status_note: IBM newsroom, Aug 19, 2026: reaffirms 'IBM Quantum Starling in 2029' and reports joining two cryogenic modules into a single environment below 15 millikelvin, an intermediate hardware step toward Starling.

claim: IBM Quantum Kookaburra, scheduled on our roadmap for 2026, will be the first quantum processor module capable of storing information in a qLDPC memory and processing it with an attached LPU
source_title: How IBM will build the world's first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer

claim: in 2025, we're building IBM Quantum Loon, a quantum chip with more connectivity and the architecture to enable proof-of-concept experiments toward high-rate qLDPC codes
source_title: How IBM will build the world's first large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer
status_note: IBM newsroom, Nov 12, 2025, unveiled 'IBM Quantum Loon, its experimental processor that, for the first time, shows that IBM has demonstrated all the key processor components needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing.'

claim: IBM Nighthawk is expected to be delivered to IBM users by the end of 2025
source_title: IBM Delivers New Quantum Processors, Software, and Algorithm Breakthroughs on Path to Advantage and Fault Tolerance
status_note: The Quantum Insider, Jan 13, 2026: 'customers on its Premium and Flex cloud plans now have early access to ibm_miami, the first quantum processing unit built on the Nighthawk design.' First sourced availability is early access reported Jan 13, 2026, after the end-2025 target; no source shows delivery by Dec 31, 2025.

claim: IBM anticipates that the first cases of verified quantum advantage will be confirmed by the wider community by the end of 2026.

status_note: IBM newsroom, Jul 30, 2026: IBM and UChicago report a 70-logical-qubit computation 'beyond the reach of leading classical simulation methods'. This is IBM's own claim; confirmation by the wider community, as the original promise specifies, is not yet shown in a source on this ledger.
